figures.caption: Figure 1: F1 score vs. dimensionality d for three graph topologies and three sample sizes. Shaded bands show ±1 standard deviation over 20 seeds.

Table 2: Incremental ablation on the 11-node cascade network (d=11, α=0.01, mean over 10 seeds). Each row adds one feature to the previous configuration. The pattern is consistent across sample sizes: AR(1)-residualized dcor and MCI pruning are the key components.

Figure 2: Elbe River main branch (d=12, 11 true edges). Left: ground truth chain. Center: CEDAR single run—nonstationarity confounds discovery (0 TP, 14 FP). Right: CEDAR + PELT—low-flow regime exposes clean causal signal, recovering 10 of 11 edges (F1=0.833). Green: TP, orange: FP, red dashed: FN.
Figure 3: CEDAR’s discovered graph vs. ground truth (seed 42). Green: TP, red dashed: FN, orange: FP.

Table 5: Named benchmarks (mean±s.e. over 5 seeds). All methods use partial correlation at α = 0.01 except the 5-node nonlinear benchmark, which uses SplitKCI. Metrics report cross-variable edges only (self-loops excluded); CEDAR assumes AR(1) self-dynamics by design and adds selfloops for all variables without validation, so including them would count as false positives for variables without true self-lags. Confounded-trends: CEDAR, CDNOTS, and CDNOTS+ use include_C=True, c_preset=linear+quad; PCMCI+ has no C-node support.
Figure 4: Structural Hamming distance (lower is better) vs. dimensionality d for three graph topologies and three sample sizes. Same layout as Figure 1.

Table 9: Stress tests under assumption violations (d=15–20, T=300, mean over 10 seeds). The gap between CEDAR and CDNOTS+ grows as violations accumulate, but CEDAR degrades predictably rather than catastrophically.

Table 10: SYPI-all-targets vs. CEDAR (mean F1 over 10 seeds, max _lag=3, ParCorr). SYPIall-targets uses LassoCV lag selection, α1=α2=0.05, no MCI pruning. CEDAR-no-MCI uses AR(1)-residualized dcor, α=0.01, no MCI pruning. Full CEDAR adds stable MCI pruning. Mean precision of SYPI-all-targets is 0.34; of Full CEDAR is 0.87.

Figure 5: Elbe River discharge (upstream station, S166) with PELT-detected regime segmentation into three hydrological regimes. Low-flow periods provide the cleanest causal signal due to reduced transient rainfall confounding.

Table 11: Elbe River benchmark (d=12, T=11,688, 11 true edges). Regime-conditional discovery substantially outperforms single-run baselines. Low-flow yields the highest precision for CEDAR, consistent with reduced transient confounding.
